newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FEATURE - Prague taxi drivers ready to take you for a ride.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Prague taxi drivers ready to take you for a ride.

text.p: Visitors to Prague from October 15 had better beware. From Tuesday local taxi drivers can happily rip you off, and it will all be completely legal.
Cabbies in the historic city will overtake the Czech banking and housing sectors, plus large tracts of local industry, by achieving complete price deregulation.
In other words they can demand as much as they like, and already Prague taxi drivers have a formula for charging foreigners: think of a number, double it and maybe add some zeros.
"Well, hotels have double prices (for foreigners) so why shouldn't we?" said one cabbie waiting for tourists near the gothic and baroque Old Town Square.
Mayor Jan Koukal washes his hands of the price deregulation, the latest idea from Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's free-market government.

"The Ministry of Finance is forcing all cities to stop regulation of prices," said Koukal, a party colleague of Klaus. "It doesn't mean that we are happy with that solution (but) it's the responsibility of the Ministry of Finance."
Under the Finance Minstry edict, the only protection left for the customer will be a requirement that prices per kilometre (mile) be posted in bold letters on taxi doors.

Prague, scarcely touched by the wars which ravaged the rest of central Europe in recent centuries, has become a huge tourist destination since the 1989 fall of communism ended bureaucracy and visas for most visitors.
Visitors -- predominantly foreigners -- clocked up three million overnight stays in the Czech capital in the first half of this year, up 33 percent from the same period in 1995.
But even in the old days when the communists regulated nearly eveything, taking advantage of tourists was common.
No self-respecting Prague taxi driver would accept local crowns, only German marks.
These days, thanks to Klaus, the Czech currency is fully convertible for tourists, and cabbies are happy to take crowns. But they do want a lot of them.

Pre-deregulation the official fare is Czech crowns (45 U.S. cents) a kilometre. But when it comes to foreigners -- particularly when they don't seem to know their way around town -- many Prague cabbies suffer from terrible amnesia. They forget to switch the meter on.
Other drivers with greater technical skills happily turn on the meter. But it tends to whirr round rather fast.
As one example among thousands, a German woman two years ago had to pay the equivalent of $120 for a ride from the airport. At the official rate, it should have cost $20.

Hotels, almost as a matter of course, charge tourists double or treble the rate they offer locals. Taking advantage of the legendary difficulty of the Czech language, some pubs display signs saying "Domaci Polovic" -- locals pay half price.
Most Western visitors earn far more than double the average Czech wage of 8,000 crowns ($300) a month.
But some Prague cabbies are thinking more in terms of four times the old fares than double.
"In Germany it costs 2.2 to 2.5 marks per kilometre so we can charge foreigners 40 crowns per kilometre, can't we?" said another cabbie just off Old Town Square.

The difference is that in Germany you will ride in a spotless Mercedes. In Prague you may get a clapped-out old Skoda, more than likely decorated with pictures of scantily- clad women awaiting your visit to a local "night club".
Some Prague cabbies are scrupulously honest but to the bewildered foreigner, they seem a minority.

To be fair to the drivers, the old official fares are ludicrously cheap. While prices of fuel, servicing and the general cost of living have risen sharply, fares have stayed almost unchanged for 3-1/2 years.
But who will come to the customer's rescue?

Last spring the consumer watchdog, the Czech Trading Inspectorate, announced it would levy heavy fines on hotels which charged more for foreigners. But just before the ruling came into effect the government overruled the inspectorate.
Mayor Koukal does have some helpful advice to tourists worried about taxis -- avoid them.

"We are trying to offer also other services...together with the airport authority we opened three more types of (bus) service from the airport to the city with a fixed fare," he said. "So there is another possibility for those people not to use taxis," he added.
Indeed, public transport in Prague is widely praised for its speed, reliability and affordability.
But for those tourists who are lost, foot-sore or just in a hurry to get back to the hotel, there are 7,000 Prague cabbies just waiting to take you for a ride. ($1=27.14 Czech Crown)
